description: Software & data builder passionate about space! I lead clear strategy & fast prototyping for NASA challenges. Looking for UI/UX designers & pitch storytellers. Let's build something stellar!
summary: Horizon is a field-advisor web app plus a seeding robot prototype. Farmers often choose what to plant by intuition and experience, and one wrong choice can cost a whole season. In Horizon, a farmer draws their real field on a satellite map, picks a crop and a planting month, and the app checks that plan against real NASA data: NASA POWER climatology (temperature, rain, soil wetness, sunshine), MODIS land cover (is this really farmland?) and MODIS NDVI (is the field bare or growing right now?). The app can disagree: it gives a score out of 100, explains why in plain words, and recommends the best month, the best crops and a better place nearby. The farmer always has the final say. A locked plan becomes a row-by-row seeding route for our autonomous tractor prototype, built with ESP32 boards and 3D-printed parts. Horizon uses free NASA data with no login, so it works for small farms anywhere on Earth.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Horizon helps a farmer decide what to plant, where and when, using real NASA data.

1. Draw the field: the farmer draws the field (any shape) on a satellite map. Areas that are too big (over 3000 ha) or mostly city or water (checked with NASA MODIS land cover) are rejected.

2. Choose: the farmer picks a crop and a planting month.

3. Check: the app pulls NASA POWER climatology for that exact location and compares it with simple crop rules (temperature range, water needs per season). It gives a score out of 100, explains the reasons in plain words, shows the best planting month, the best crops for that field, and a better spot nearby if one exists. It also shows live MODIS NDVI (how green the field is now) with a plain-word verdict.

4. Decide: the farmer can follow the advice or keep their own plan. The decision is saved in the plan.

5. Seed: the locked plan becomes a predictable row-by-row seeding route (straight lines and 90-degree turns, a seed drop about every 25 cm, only inside the field shape), plus real-field numbers (seed kg, number of rows, row spacing).

THE ROBOT PROTOTYPE

An autonomous seeding tractor: ESP32 DevKit brain, 4 DC gear motors with tank (skid) steering through an L298N driver, a servo seed dropper, a 3D-printed body (designed in Onshape), powered by a 1S lithium pack with a TP4056 charger and a 5V boost converter. It runs the route by dead reckoning and can also be driven over its own Wi-Fi from a browser. A base-station firmware (ESP32-C3) links the web app to the tractor over Bluetooth and ESP-NOW radio.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Fewer lost seasons: the farmer is warned before planting, not after.

- Free and simple: NASA POWER and MODIS need no login, the app runs in any browser, and the robot uses cheap hobby parts.

- Works anywhere: only the data location changes, so it is not limited to Uzbekistan.

- Next step: a market-balance check that compares what all farmers have planted with national demand, so the app can warn about oversupply (price crashes) and recommend crops that will be in short supply.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet maps, Web Bluetooth, Web Serial; C++ (Arduino core for ESP32); ESP32 DevKit, ESP32-C3, L298N, DC gear motors, SG90 servo, LiPo + TP4056 + boost converter; Onshape (CAD), Ultimaker Cura and FDM 3D printing (PETG); Claude (AI assistant) for help with code and documentation.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Honest limits: NASA POWER is about 50 km resolution, MODIS land cover 500 m and NDVI 250 m, so field detail comes from MODIS. The crop rules are simplified agronomy, a first check, not a replacement for a local agronomist. The robot is a table-top prototype that drives by timing, not GPS. The farmer always has the final decision.
